subject: physics

items.q: Which statement gives the specification's definition of the specific heat capacity of a substance?
items.correct: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
items.misconception: The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of the whole sample by one degree Celsius.
items.why: The bigger block really does need more energy for the same temperature rise, so students attach that fact to c instead of to m. The word 'specific' is not everyday language, and its technical meaning — 'per kilogram' — is easy to skip over. The mass is already accounted for separately, by m in the equation. 'Specific' means the quantity has been divided by mass, so c is fixed for a given substance; doubling the mass doubles ∆E through m and leaves c untouched.
items.random_wrong: The thermal energy stored by one kilogram of the substance at a temperature of one degree Celsius.

items.q: Which word equation does the specification give for the energy change when a system's temperature changes?
items.correct: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
items.misconception: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity ÷ change in temperature
items.why: Students move the symbol nearest the equals sign and stop, and read left to right the expression ∆E ÷ m × ∆θ still looks as though ∆θ has been dealt with. Missing brackets hide the error. Anything multiplying c on one side divides the other side, and here two quantities multiply c. Write the bracket in — c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) — and check the units: J ÷ (kg × °C) is J/kg °C, which is the unit of c.
items.random_wrong: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × final temperature

items.q: A beaker holds 300 g of water at 80 °C. The water is heated until it reaches 100 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the change in thermal energy of the water?
items.why: Balances in the laboratory read in grams, and students are used to the number they measured being the number they use. The 'per kilogram' hidden inside J/kg °C is not visible in the symbol equation itself. The unit of c fixes the unit of m: because c is joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, m must be in kilograms. Convert first, then sanity-check the size of the answer — 300 g of water cannot need millions of joules for a modest temperature rise.

items.q: Water is heated from 18 °C to 78 °C. Which value should be used for ∆θ in ∆E = m c ∆θ, and why?
items.correct: 60 °C, because ∆θ means the change in the temperature.
items.misconception: 78 °C, because ∆θ is the temperature that the water reaches.
items.why: The final temperature is what the thermometer actually shows at the end, so it feels like 'the' temperature of the experiment. The ∆ symbol is easily read as decoration rather than as an instruction to subtract. ∆ always means 'change in'. Do the subtraction first and write that number down before touching the equation. Check it against a case where nothing happens: water left at 18 °C stores no extra energy, and only the subtraction gives ∆θ = 0.
items.random_wrong: 351 K, because temperatures must be converted into kelvin first.

items.q: A 250 g metal block is heated by an immersion heater. The joulemeter shows that 10 000 J has been transferred and the block's temperature rises by 20 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J/kg °C?
items.why: Students move the symbol nearest the equals sign and stop, and read left to right the expression ∆E ÷ m × ∆θ still looks as though ∆θ has been dealt with. Missing brackets hide the error. Anything multiplying c on one side divides the other side, and here two quantities multiply c. Write the bracket in — c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) — and check the units: J ÷ (kg × °C) is J/kg °C, which is the unit of c.

items.q: Which line gives the units the specification uses for the quantities in ∆E = m c ∆θ?
items.correct: ∆E in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, ∆θ in °C
items.misconception: ∆E in J, m in kg, c in J/kg °C, ∆θ in kelvin
items.why: Kelvin conversion is drilled hard in the particle model and gas content, so it becomes a reflex applied to every temperature that appears in any equation. Check the unit of c: it is per degree Celsius, so ∆θ must be in degrees Celsius to match. A change of one degree Celsius happens to be the same size as a change of one kelvin, but the units the specification states here are °C.
items.random_wrong: ∆E in J, m in kg, c in J per °C, ∆θ in °C

items.q: A hot metal block of mass m cools from 90 °C to 30 °C in still air. What does ∆E = m c ∆θ tell you about the block?
items.correct: The block's thermal energy store has fallen by m × c × 60, and that energy is released.
items.misconception: Nothing at all, because the equation applies only while a system is being heated up.
items.why: Almost every worked example met in lessons involves a heater, and 'thermal energy' is spoken of as something gained. Cooling then looks like a different phenomenon needing a different equation. The equation is symmetric. A fall of 60 °C releases exactly the energy that a rise of 60 °C would store for the same object, and the specification's own wording — 'stored in or released from' — makes that explicit.
items.random_wrong: Its temperature has fallen, but the energy stored in the block has not changed at all.

items.q: Water has a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C and aluminium has 900 J/kg °C. What does this tell you?
items.correct: Warming 1 kg of water by 1 °C needs more energy than warming 1 kg of aluminium.
items.misconception: Water heats up faster than aluminium does when both are supplied with the same energy.
items.why: The everyday sense of 'high capacity' is 'does a lot', so a big number sounds like a big or fast temperature change. The per-degree structure of the quantity is not carried by the word itself. Read the definition literally: c is the energy needed for each degree of rise, for each kilogram. A big c therefore means a stubborn substance — a lot of energy for a small rise. Rearranging to ∆θ = ∆E ÷ (m c) puts c on the bottom, where its effect is visible.
items.random_wrong: A kilogram of water always contains more thermal energy than a kilogram of aluminium.

items.q: In Required practical activity 1, how is the specific heat capacity of the metal block calculated?
items.correct: By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the temperature rise.
items.misconception: By dividing the energy supplied by the temperature rise of the block only.
items.why: Students move the symbol nearest the equals sign and stop, and read left to right the expression ∆E ÷ m × ∆θ still looks as though ∆θ has been dealt with. Missing brackets hide the error. Anything multiplying c on one side divides the other side, and here two quantities multiply c. Write the bracket in — c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ) — and check the units: J ÷ (kg × °C) is J/kg °C, which is the unit of c.
items.random_wrong: By dividing the energy supplied by the mass and by the starting temperature of the block.

items.q: A student heats a metal block with an immersion heater but does not insulate it. The energy supplied is measured accurately with a joulemeter. What is the effect on the calculated value of the specific heat capacity?
items.correct: It is too high, because some energy warms the room and the temperature rise is smaller.
items.misconception: There is no effect, because all the energy from the heater goes into the block.
items.why: The joulemeter reading is a single definite number, and it is easy to treat a measured value as the value that arrived at the destination. Energy transferred to the surroundings leaves no visible trace. The measured energy is the energy supplied, not the energy that arrived. Insulating the block and starting close to room temperature reduce the difference but never remove it, which is why the practical has to be evaluated as well as performed.
items.random_wrong: It is too low, because the block has gained less energy than the heater supplied.

items.q: Which set of measurements is needed to determine the specific heat capacity of the block in this practical?
items.correct: The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the temperature rise.
items.misconception: The mass of the block, the energy supplied by the heater, and the final temperature.
items.why: The starting temperature is often just room temperature, so it feels like background information rather than data, while the final reading is taken at the dramatic end of the experiment. The equation contains ∆θ, so a subtraction is unavoidable and both readings are data. Record the starting temperature before switching the heater on, and keep reading for a short time afterwards, as the block goes on warming briefly.
items.random_wrong: The mass of the block, the power of the heater, and the temperature rise.

items.q: Two identical 1 kg blocks of the same metal are heated. Block X rises by 10 °C and block Y rises by 30 °C. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Block Y needed three times as much energy as X, because ∆E is proportional to ∆θ.
items.misconception: Block Y has three times the specific heat capacity of X, because it became three times hotter.
items.why: The bigger block really does need more energy for the same temperature rise, so students attach that fact to c instead of to m. The word 'specific' is not everyday language, and its technical meaning — 'per kilogram' — is easy to skip over. The mass is already accounted for separately, by m in the equation. 'Specific' means the quantity has been divided by mass, so c is fixed for a given substance; doubling the mass doubles ∆E through m and leaves c untouched.
items.random_wrong: Both blocks needed the same energy, because they have the same mass and are the same metal.

items.q: A block cools from 90 °C to 30 °C. Has the energy stored in it changed?
items.correct: Yes. Its temperature has fallen, so the energy in its thermal store has fallen by m c ∆θ, and that energy has been transferred to the surroundings.
items.misconception: Temperature and thermal energy are separate things, so a falling temperature need not mean the stored energy has changed.
items.why: Temperature is the quantity students actually measure and energy is invisible, so the two are easily held apart. The equation links them, but only if ∆θ is read as evidence of an energy change. For a given system a temperature change is exactly the observable sign of a change in the thermal energy store, and ∆E = m c ∆θ gives the size of that change. No temperature change means no ∆E; a temperature change always means one.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A 1 kg block of metal is at 30 °C. Does m c × 30 give the energy stored in the block?
items.correct: No. ∆E = m c ∆θ gives a change in the thermal energy store, not the total energy the block stores.
items.misconception: Specific heat capacity is the total thermal energy a substance stores, so the energy is just mass × specific heat capacity and the temperature change ∆θ does not need to be included.
items.why: The equation looks like a formula for a quantity rather than for a change, and the ∆ signs are easily dropped when the symbols are copied down. Students also expect an energy value to be a total, as it is for many other stores. Both ∆ symbols matter, and they matter together: a change in temperature gives a change in energy. A total would need a zero point for the energy, and the specification never provides one.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
items.correct: Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C.
items.misconception: The unit is J/°C, because specific heat capacity is the energy needed for each degree of temperature rise.
items.why: Students remember the 'per degree Celsius' half of the definition, which is the part repeated most often in class, while the 'per kilogram' half is carried only by the word 'specific'. Build the unit straight from the definition: energy (J), for one kilogram (/kg), for one degree Celsius (°C). Both 'per' phrases are in the definition, so both must appear in the unit.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student rearranges ∆E = m c ∆θ and writes c = (m × ∆θ) ÷ ∆E. What has gone wrong?
items.correct: The expression has been turned upside down; the correct rearrangement is c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).
items.misconception: When a quantity is made the subject, whatever shared its side of the equation goes on top of the fraction.
items.why: Rearranging is often done by pattern-matching remembered triangles rather than by doing the same operation to both sides, and the reciprocal looks equally tidy on the page. Divide both sides by m ∆θ and see what survives: ∆E ÷ (m ∆θ) = c. A unit check catches the slip at once, because kg °C/J is not the unit of specific heat capacity.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: An uninsulated block transfers energy to the room. Is the calculated specific heat capacity too high or too low?
items.correct: Too high, because the recorded temperature rise is smaller than the measured energy supply should have produced, and ∆θ is on the bottom of c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).
items.misconception: Losing energy must make the answer too small, because energy has been lost from the experiment.
items.why: 'Energy lost' and 'value too low' feel like the same idea, so students judge the direction of the error from the word rather than from where the affected quantity sits in the equation. Ask which measured quantity the transfer actually changes. The joulemeter reading is unaffected, but the temperature rise is reduced, and dividing by a smaller ∆θ makes c come out larger.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student records the mass, the temperature rise and the power marked on the immersion heater. Can the specific heat capacity be found?
items.correct: No. Power is energy per second, so the heating time must be measured as well: ∆E = power × time.
items.misconception: The power of the heater is the energy it has supplied, so no timing is needed.
items.why: The power is printed on the heater as a single definite number, and both power and energy are spoken of loosely as 'how much the heater gives out'. In lessons a joulemeter often replaces the calculation, so the time never has to be used explicitly. Check the units: a 50 W heater supplies 50 J each second, so the joules depend on how long it runs. Either read the energy directly from a joulemeter, or measure the time and use energy = power × time before substituting into c = ∆E ÷ (m × ∆θ).
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.1.1.3 Energy changes in systems
